Why do the men carry on despite the terrible smell?

Under ordinary circumstances such a stench would have brought our enterprise to an end; but this was no ordinary case, and the high and terrible purpose in which we were involved gave us a strength which rose above merely physical considerations. After the involuntary shrinking consequent on the first nauseous whiff, we one and all set about our work as though that loathsome place were a garden of roses.
Their serious purpose gave them strength beyond physical feelings. After the first nasty whiff, they all set to work as if the place were a garden of roses.

In the library I found, to my great delight, a vast number of English books, whole shelves full of them, and bound volumes of magazines and newspapers. A table in the centre was littered with English magazines and newspapers, though none of them were of very recent date. The books were of the most varied kind--history, geography, politics, political economy, botany, geology, law--all relating to England and English life and customs and manners. There were even such books of reference as the London Directory, the "Red" and "Blue" books, Whitaker's Almanac, the Army and Navy Lists, and--it somehow gladdened my heart to see it--the Law List.

What does the narrator find in the library, and what does it suggest?
He finds shelves of English books and magazines about history, law, geography and daily life, plus directories and almanacs. It suggests the owner has been studying England carefully.

Why does Chyavana make a promise to the twins, and what happens to them?

"Having obtained coveted beauty and also his wife, Chyavana, of exceeding energy, well pleased, spake these words unto the nose-born celestials: 'Since at your hands, an old man, I have obtained youth, and beauty, and also this wife of mine, I will, well pleased, make you quaffers of the Soma juice in the presence of the lord of celestials himself. This I tell you truly.' Hearing this, highly delighted, the twins ascendedto heaven; and Chyavana and Sukanya too passed their days happily even like celestials."
He is pleased that they gave him youth, beauty and his wife. In return he promises them a share of the Soma juice, and the twins go happily to heaven.

On Monday, Sharmila watched the football game from the wall and kicked at the dust, wishing someone would ask her. On Tuesday, a girl named Minakshi waved and called, "Come, you can be the goalkeeper!" Sharmila's shoulders dropped and warmth spread through her, as if the ground had finally made room. She dived at the first ball and missed, and nobody minded. On Thursday, a new child stood at the wall. Sharmila ran over and called, "Come, you can be the goalkeeper!"

Why does Sharmila say the same words to the new child at the end?
She remembers how it felt to wait at the wall and then be invited. Now she passes on the same kindness by calling the new child to be goalkeeper.

How does Pooja make herself happy in the waiting room?

In the clinic waiting room, Pooja was bored. The queue was long. Lalremsiami, her mother, handed her an empty paper cup from the water cooler. Pooja held it to her ear. 'Hello, Nani?' Then she put it on her finger. 'This is a tiny hat.' She turned it upside down on the chair. 'A cake! Happy birthday, Mumma.' A boy nearby watched, so she made it a trumpet and tooted.
She plays pretend with the empty paper cup, using it as a phone, a tiny hat, a cake and a trumpet. This turns a boring wait into a game, and a boy nearby watches her.

In the project review at the design agency, the room grew tense. Farida insisted the client had changed the brief in the second week; others remembered it in the fourth. Ojas, who was leading the review, had his own clear memory: the third week, on a phone call. He felt tempted to settle it with his own certainty. Instead he said, "I remember it as week three, on a call. But I'm not sure memory is the best judge here." He opened the shared inbox. The client's email was dated day nine: week two. Farida had been right. Ojas nodded at her. "Your memory wins. Mine was off by a week." Then he added a line to the process notes: 'Log every brief change in writing the same day.'

How does Ojas settle the disagreement in the review?
He admits his own memory could be wrong and checks the shared inbox. The client's email shows Farida was right, so he accepts it and adds a note to log changes in writing the same day.

Why does Alka thank her old teacher in this letter?

Dear Jasleen Ma'am, It's been a year since I finished my apprenticeship in your carpentry workshop, and I have a confession. For my first six months at the new job, I talked exactly like you. "Measure twice, cut once, beta." "The wood tells you where it wants to split." I even called my apprentice "beta", and he's older than me! Your phrases made me feel like I knew what I was doing when I didn't yet. Lately I've noticed some of them don't sound like me. I don't say "beta". I explain things with drawings, not proverbs. But "measure twice" stays forever. It's the best advice anyone ever gave me. So thank you for lending me your voice until I found mine. With respect, Alka
Using Jasleen Ma'am's phrases gave her confidence before she felt skilled, like borrowing a voice. Now she has found her own way of explaining, but she keeps "measure twice" as the best advice.

"Ishita, what do you want for dinner? Dal-rice or chapati-sabzi?" "I don't know." "Pick one, beta." "I don't KNOW, Mummy!" "Okay, okay. Do you want to wear your blue nightdress or the pink one?" "I don't care!" "Ishita, what's wrong?" "Everything! School was so long. We had the test, then dance practice, then the bus was late." "Okay. Come here." "And now everyone keeps asking me things." "You're tired. Your brain is full. How about I choose tonight?" "...Yes." "Dal-rice and the blue nightdress." "Okay." "And tomorrow morning, when you're fresh, you can choose your lunch."

Why can't Ishita choose her dinner?
She is tired after a long school day with a test, dance practice and a late bus. Her brain is full, so even small choices feel too much. Her mother chooses for tonight and lets her choose tomorrow.

How is Rafiq teaching Uma to open the lid?

Rafiq twisted the tiffin lid off. "Watch, Uma. Twist and pop." "Twist!" Uma grabbed the raisin box and turned it hard. The lid stayed shut. "Abbu did. Twist," Uma said, and turned it again, the same way. "Almost, jaan. Look at my hand. Other way." Uma frowned at the box, then at Rafiq's fingers. "Want to see it slowly?" "Again!" Uma said.
He shows her, then helps her notice that she turns it the wrong way. He asks her to watch his hand and offers to show it slowly, and Uma wants to try again.

Hemant: Zoya, you're still glaring at me. It was only a pen. Zoya: Don't talk to me right now. My face is hot. If I speak, I'll say something mean. Hemant: So what will you do? Zoya: I'll read my book till lunch is over. Later, when I'm not shaking, I'll think about it properly. Hemant: That's your whole plan? Zoya: If I answer now it becomes a bigger fight. Later I can work out if I'm angry about the pen or about how you grabbed it. Hemant: Fine. I'll be under the tree. Zoya: Good. Not yet, Hemant.

What is Zoya's plan for handling her anger?
She will not talk while her face is hot, because she might say something mean. She will read until lunch ends and think later about whether she is angry about the pen or the way it was grabbed.

Why did Maria never ask questions at first?

At the community centre's evening computer lab, Maria was the oldest student at twenty-two. She had dropped out of college and now worked at a shop, but she wanted to learn data analysis. Siddharth, the volunteer instructor, noticed she took notes on everything but never asked questions. One day he asked her why. "I don't want to look stupid," she said. He smiled. "Asking is how you learn." He suggested she set small weekly goals: one new function, one practice dataset. He also showed her how to explain back what she'd learned. Maria started asking questions, and she built a small dashboard tracking the shop's sales. Her manager asked her to present it. She was nervous, but she did.
She was afraid of looking stupid. Siddharth told her that asking is how you learn and suggested small weekly goals. After that she began asking questions and built a sales dashboard.

The art room at the community centre in Bhopal was open on Saturday mornings. Rehana, nine, came in to draw a picture for a competition. She forgot about the competition almost at once. She was drawing the old banyan tree outside the window, root by root, twig by twig. She didn't hear the bell for snack. She didn't notice Anjali, the art volunteer, standing behind her. "Rehana, the entries were due at eleven. It's twelve now." Rehana looked up, blinking. "Oh." Then she looked back at the roots. "Can I finish it anyway? I just want to see how it looks." Anjali smiled and pulled up a chair. "Go on. I want to see too."

What happens when Rehana misses the entry deadline?
She gets so absorbed in drawing the banyan tree that she forgets the competition. Anjali does not scold her. She lets Rehana finish and pulls up a chair to watch.

Why is Kishore thanking Pranav?

'Pranav-bhaiya, got a minute?' 'Kishore! How did the interview go?' 'That's why I'm here. First, thank you. Properly. That mock interview on Saturday was brutal.' 'Too brutal?' 'No. When you said my answers sounded like I'd memorised a website, I wanted to disappear.' 'Sorry about that.' 'Don't be. I went home and rewrote all of them with my own examples. The canteen inventory thing, the robotics club budget. And today when they asked about teamwork, I told the robotics story.' 'And?' 'They asked me three follow-ups on it. They were actually interested.' 'That's great, man.' 'Second round is Friday. Can I tell you how it goes?' 'You'd better. Most people take the mock and I never hear from them again.' Kishore grinned, a bit red in the face. 'Not me, bhaiya.'
Pranav's blunt mock interview made him rewrite his answers with his own examples, like the robotics club budget. At the real interview this worked, and the panel asked interested follow-up questions.

In the village, the doctor's jeep had come twice in one week, and nine-year-old Chaitanya had started lying awake. He heard whispers at night: "hospital," "the town," "we'll see." In the morning everyone smiled too much. One evening, his mother, Rashmi, found him sitting on the cattle-shed wall, very still. "Chaitu, you're worried about Dadaji." He nodded. "Is he going to die?" Rashmi sat beside him. "Dadaji's heart is tired and weak, and the doctor wants him in the big hospital in town so they can watch him closely. We don't know everything yet. When I know more, I'll tell you. I promise." Chaitanya thought. "I thought it was worse. Because everyone was whispering." "No more whispering. You can ask me anything." "Can I go see him?" "Sunday. We'll take the bus together."

How does Rashmi handle Chaitanya's worry?

She explains simply that Dadaji's heart is weak and he needs hospital care, admits she does not know everything and promises to tell him more. She ends the whispering and promises a bus trip to visit on Sunday.

How do Arohi and Sudha solve their second quarrel?

"It's my turn on the swing!" "No, mine!" Arohi and Sudha were both holding the chain. Their cousin Tenzin wandered over with a coin. "Heads, Arohi. Tails, Sudha. Okay?" "...Okay." The coin spun. Tails. Arohi pouted but let go, and Sudha swung high. Two days later, the same two were fighting over the last mango ice lolly. "Mine!" "I saw it first!" Arohi stopped. "Wait. Tenzin's coin way. Heads me, tails you?" Sudha blinked. "Okay." Nani flipped a coin for them. Heads. Arohi grinned, and broke off the end for Sudha anyway.
They remember Tenzin's coin trick and ask Nani to flip a coin for the last ice lolly. Arohi wins the toss but still breaks off a piece for Sudha.

The school hall was packed for Monday assembly, and Ritu's hands were damp around her three index cards. Her topic: why the school should start a recycling drive. Backstage, Afreen squeezed her arm. "Remember the plan. Story, three points, one ask." Ritu walked to the mic. Four hundred faces. Her mind went blank for a second. She looked at the first card: "The bin behind the canteen." "Last week," she began, "I counted forty plastic bottles in one bin behind our canteen." A few students looked up. Her voice steadied. She made her three points, pausing after each, and ended: "Bring one bottle to the green box on Friday." Afreen was clapping hardest. On Friday, the green box was overflowing.

How does Ritu manage her nerves during her speech?
She follows the plan: a story, three points and one ask. When her mind goes blank, she looks at her first card and begins with the bottle count, and her voice steadies.

There was a rapid patter of bare feet, and an unseen hand opened the door into the huntsmen's room, from which came the clear sounds of a balalayka on which someone, who was evidently a master of the art, was playing. Natasha had been listening to those strains for some time and now went out into the passage to hear better.

What is Natasha listening to, and what does she do about it?
She hears someone playing a balalayka very skilfully in the huntsmen's room. She has listened for some time and now goes out into the passage to hear it better.

What happens to Tushin when he enters the hut?

All were silent. Tushin appeared at the threshold and made his way timidly from behind the backs of the generals. As he stepped past the generals in the crowded hut, feeling embarrassed as he always was by the sight of his superiors, he did not notice the staff of the banner and stumbled over it. Several of those present laughed.
He feels embarrassed, as he always does before his superiors, and makes his way timidly past the generals. He does not notice the banner's staff and stumbles over it, and some people laugh.

The conflagration, at which he had looked with so much indifference the evening before, had greatly increased during the night. Moscow was on fire in several places. The buildings in Carriage Row, across the river, in the Bazaar and the Povarskoy, as well as the barges on the Moskva River and the timber yards by the Dorogomilov Bridge, were all ablaze.

What does this passage tell us about Moscow that morning?
The fire he watched the evening before has grown during the night. Moscow is burning in several places, including Carriage Row, the Bazaar, the barges on the river and the timber yards.

What do Prince Andrew and the officer see as they ride past the village?

Having ridden beyond the village, continually meeting and overtaking soldiers and officers of various regiments, they saw on their left some entrenchments being thrown up, the freshly dug clay of which showed up red. Several battalions of soldiers, in their shirt sleeves despite the cold wind, swarmed in these earthworks like a host of white ants; spadefuls of red clay were continually being thrown up from behind the bank by unseen hands. Prince Andrew and the officer rode up, looked at the entrenchment, and went on again. Just behind it they came upon some dozens of soldiers, continually replaced by others, who ran from the entrenchment. They had to hold their noses and put their horses to a trot to escape from the poisoned atmosphere of these latrines.
They see soldiers in shirt sleeves digging fresh red clay earthworks, swarming like white ants. Behind them the smell from the latrines is so foul that they hold their noses and trot away.

At last, passage paid, and luggage safe, we stood on board the schooner. Hoisting sail, it glided down the Acushnet river. On one side, New Bedford rose in terraces of streets, their ice-covered trees all glittering in the clear, cold air. Huge hills and mountains of casks on casks were piled upon her wharves, and side by side the world-wandering whale ships lay silent and safely moored at last; while from others came a sound of carpenters and coopers, with blended noises of fires and forges to melt the pitch, all betokening that new cruises were on the start; that one most perilous and long voyage ended, only begins a second; and a second ended, only begins a third, and so on, for ever and for aye. Such is the endlessness, yea, the intolerableness of all earthly effort.

What does the writer think the busy scene at the wharves shows?
He sees ships and workshops getting ready for new voyages, so that one finished journey only begins another. He calls this the endlessness of all earthly effort.

How does the man behave in the boat, and how does he take advice?

He put his pipe back in his mouth with an undisturbed expression of face, and sat as composed and contented as if we were already out of England. Yet he was as submissive to a word of advice as if he had been in constant terror; for, when we ran ashore to get some bottles of beer into the boat, and he was stepping out, I hinted that I thought he would be safest where he was, and he said. "Do you, dear boy?" and quietly sat down again.
He stays calm and contented, as if they were already out of England. Yet he takes advice at once: when told he would be safest where he was, he quietly sat down again.

In every rage of wind and rush of rain, I heard pursuers. Twice, I could have sworn there was a knocking and whispering at the outer door. With these fears upon me, I began either to imagine or recall that I had had mysterious warnings of this man's approach. That, for weeks gone by, I had passed faces in the streets which I had thought like his. That these likenesses had grown more numerous, as he, coming over the sea, had drawn nearer. That his wicked spirit had somehow sent these messengers to mine, and that now on this stormy night he was as good as his word, and with me.

What fears trouble Pip on the stormy night?
He hears pursuers in every gust and thinks someone knocks at the door. He begins to believe he had warnings of the man's approach: faces like his in the streets, more of them as the man came nearer.

Why is Pip left confused after speaking to the old gentleman?

Curious to know how the old gentleman stood informed concerning the reputation of Mr. Jaggers, I roared that name at him. He threw me into the greatest confusion by laughing heartily and replying in a very sprightly manner, "No, to be sure; you're right." And to this hour I have not the faintest notion what he meant, or what joke he thought I had made.
He shouted a name to find out how much the old man knew, and the man laughed heartily and agreed. Pip still has no idea what he meant or what joke he found.

By the wilderness of casks that I had walked on long ago, and on which the rain of years had fallen since, rotting them in many places, and leaving miniature swamps and pools of water upon those that stood on end, I made my way to the ruined garden. I went all round it; round by the corner where Herbert and I had fought our battle; round by the paths where Estella and I had walked. So cold, so lonely, so dreary all!

What does Pip see as he walks through the old brewery and garden?

He finds rotting casks with small pools of water on them and a ruined garden. He goes round the corner where he fought Herbert and the paths where he walked with Estella, and finds it all cold, lonely and dreary.

What does Mrs. Fairfax believe Mr. Rochester has gone to London to do?

I was going back to Thornfield: but how long was I to stay there? Not long; of that I was sure. I had heard from Mrs. Fairfax in the interim of my absence: the party at the hall was dispersed; Mr. Rochester had left for London three weeks ago, but he was then expected to return in a fortnight. Mrs. Fairfax surmised that he was gone to make arrangements for his wedding, as he had talked of purchasing a new carriage: she said the idea of his marrying Miss Ingram still seemed strange to her; but from what everybody said, and from what she had herself seen, she could no longer doubt that the event would shortly take place. "You would be strangely incredulous if you did doubt it," was my mental comment. "I don't doubt it."
She thinks he is arranging his wedding, since he talked of buying a new carriage. It seems strange to her that he will marry Miss Ingram, but she no longer doubts it will happen soon.

I felt a burning glow mount to my face; for bitter and agitating recollections were awakened by the allusion to marriage. They all saw the embarrassment and the emotion. Diana and Mary relieved me by turning their eyes elsewhere than to my crimsoned visage; but the colder and sterner brother continued to gaze, till the trouble he had excited forced out tears as well as colour.

How do the people at the table react when Jane blushes?
Diana and Mary look away to spare her. The colder, sterner brother keeps staring until the discomfort brings tears as well as colour to her face.

Why does the wind excite Jane instead of making her sad?

Probably, if I had lately left a good home and kind parents, this would have been the hour when I should most keenly have regretted the separation; that wind would then have saddened my heart; this obscure chaos would have disturbed my peace! as it was, I derived from both a strange excitement, and reckless and feverish, I wished the wind to howl more wildly, the gloom to deepen to darkness, and the confusion to rise to clamour.
She has not left a good home or kind parents, so there is no separation to regret. Instead she feels a strange, feverish excitement and wants the wind to howl and the darkness to deepen.

"A servant has had the nightmare; that is all. She's an excitable, nervous person: she construed her dream into an apparition, or something of that sort, no doubt; and has taken a fit with fright. Now, then, I must see you all back into your rooms; for, till the house is settled, she cannot be looked after. Gentlemen, have the goodness to set the ladies the example. Miss Ingram, I am sure you will not fail in evincing superiority to idle terrors. Amy and Louisa, return to your nests like a pair of doves, as you are. Mesdames" (to the dowagers), "you will take cold to a dead certainty, if you stay in this chill gallery any longer."

What does the speaker tell the guests happened, and what does he ask them to do?
He says a nervous servant had a nightmare and mistook it for a ghost. He asks everyone to go back to their rooms so the house can settle and the servant can be looked after.

Why does he want Jane to sleep in the nursery?

"And there is room enough in Adele's little bed for you. You must share it with her to-night, Jane: it is no wonder that the incident you have related should make you nervous, and I would rather you did not sleep alone: promise me to go to the nursery."
The incident she described would naturally make her nervous, and he would rather she did not sleep alone. So he asks her to share Adele's little bed.

"Rather an inhospitable question to put to a visitor; but since you ask it, I answer simply to have a little talk with you; I got tired of my mute books and empty rooms. Besides, since yesterday I have experienced the excitement of a person to whom a tale has been half-told, and who is impatient to hear the sequel."

Why does the speaker say he came to see his visitor?
He is tired of his silent books and empty rooms and wants a little talk. He is also impatient, like someone told half a tale, to hear what comes next.

What does the narrator find in Mr. Rochester's room?

Something creaked: it was a door ajar; and that door was Mr. Rochester's, and the smoke rushed in a cloud from thence. I thought no more of Mrs. Fairfax; I thought no more of Grace Poole, or the laugh: in an instant, I was within the chamber. Tongues of flame darted round the bed: the curtains were on fire. In the midst of blaze and vapour, Mr. Rochester lay stretched motionless, in deep sleep.
Smoke pours from his open door. Inside, flames leap around the bed and the curtains are on fire, while Mr. Rochester lies motionless in a deep sleep in the middle of the blaze.

"Why not?" I asked myself. "What alienates him from the house? Will he leave it again soon? Mrs. Fairfax said he seldom stayed here longer than a fortnight at a time; and he has now been resident eight weeks. If he does go, the change will be doleful. Suppose he should be absent spring, summer, and autumn: how joyless sunshine and fine days will seem!"

What is Jane worried about in this passage?
She fears Mr. Rochester may leave Thornfield again. He has stayed eight weeks, longer than his usual fortnight, and if he were away for months, even sunny days would feel joyless to her.

What does the narrator say she will do with the next eight years of her story?

Hitherto I have recorded in detail the events of my insignificant existence: to the first ten years of my life I have given almost as many chapters. But this is not to be a regular autobiography: I am only bound to invoke Memory where I know her responses will possess some degree of interest; therefore I now pass a space of eight years almost in silence: a few lines only are necessary to keep up the links of connection.
She will pass over them almost in silence. Since she is not writing a full autobiography, she will only write about what is interesting to remember and use a few lines to keep the story linked.

"I have intimated my view of the case: I am incapable of taking any other. I am not brutally selfish, blindly unjust, or fiendishly ungrateful. Besides, I am resolved I will have a home and connections. I like Moor House, and I will live at Moor House; I like Diana and Mary, and I will attach myself for life to Diana and Mary. It would please and benefit me to have five thousand pounds; it would torment and oppress me to have twenty thousand; which, moreover, could never be mine in justice, though it might in law. I abandon to you, then, what is absolutely superfluous to me. Let there be no opposition, and no discussion about it; let us agree amongst each other, and decide the point at once."

What does the speaker decide about the money, and why?
She keeps an amount that would please her and gives away the rest, which she does not need. She says she wants a home and ties with Diana and Mary more than extra money.

What is the lodge like when she arrives at Gateshead?

I reached the lodge at Gateshead about five o'clock in the afternoon of the first of May: I stepped in there before going up to the hall. It was very clean and neat: the ornamental windows were hung with little white curtains; the floor was spotless; the grate and fire-irons were burnished bright, and the fire burnt clear. Bessie sat on the hearth, nursing her last-born, and Robert and his sister played quietly in a corner.
It is very clean and neat, with white curtains, a spotless floor and a bright fire. Bessie sits by the hearth nursing her youngest child, while two other children play quietly in a corner.

The succeeding week seemed long: it came to an end at last, however, like all sublunary things, and once more, towards the close of a pleasant autumn day, I found myself afoot on the road to Lowton. A picturesque track it was, by the way; lying along the side of the beck and through the sweetest curves of the dale: but that day I thought more of the letters, that might or might not be awaiting me at the little burgh whither I was bound, than of the charms of lea and water.

What is on the narrator's mind as she walks to Lowton?
She is thinking more of the letters that may or may not be waiting for her than of the lovely path beside the stream. The week had seemed long, and she is eager for news.

Why does the Professor test the lock?

"In manus tuas, Domine!" he said, crossing himself as he passed over the threshold. We closed the door behind us, lest when we should have lit our lamps we should possibly attract attention from the road. The Professor carefully tried the lock, lest we might not be able to open it from within should we be in a hurry making our exit. Then we all lit our lamps and proceeded on our search.
He wants to be sure they can open the door from inside if they must leave in a hurry. They also close the door behind them so that lamplight will not draw attention from the road.

"I have read your letters to Miss Lucy. Forgive me, but I had to begin to inquire somewhere, and there was none to ask. I know that you were with her at Whitby. She sometimes kept a diary--you need not look surprised, Madam Mina; it was begun after you had left, and was in imitation of you--and in that diary she traces by inference certain things to a sleep-walking in which she puts down that you saved her. In great perplexity then I come to you, and ask you out of your so much kindness to tell me all of it that you can remember."

Why does Van Helsing come to Mina, and what does he ask?
He has read her letters to Lucy and Lucy's diary, which says Mina saved her during sleepwalking. He is puzzled, so he asks Mina to tell him all she can remember.

What does "Despair has its own calms" mean in this passage?

"So, my friend, you are tired? Get to bed. There is the surest rest. I may not have the pleasure to talk to-night, since there are many labours to me; but you will sleep, I pray." I passed to my room and went to bed, and, strange to say, slept without dreaming. Despair has its own calms.
The narrator goes to bed and sleeps without dreaming. The phrase means that when someone feels hopeless, there can be a strange quiet, because the worst fear has already been felt.

"She is one of God's women, fashioned by His own hand to show us men and other women that there is a heaven where we can enter, and that its light can be here on earth. So true, so sweet, so noble, so little an egoist--and that, let me tell you, is much in this age, so sceptical and selfish. And you, sir--I have read all the letters to poor Miss Lucy, and some of them speak of you, so I know you since some days from the knowing of others; but I have seen your true self since last night. You will give me your hand, will you not? And let us be friends for all our lives."

What does Van Helsing say about Mina, and what does he ask of the man he is speaking to?
He praises Mina as true, sweet and noble, and unselfish in a selfish age. He then asks the man for his hand and offers lifelong friendship.

Tell me what the speaker wants to know, and why he thinks he may ask.

"Jack Seward, I don't want to shove myself in anywhere where I've no right to be; but this is no ordinary case. You know I loved that girl and wanted to marry her; but, although that's all past and gone, I can't help feeling anxious about her all the same. What is it that's wrong with her? The Dutchman--and a fine old fellow he is; I can see that--said, that time you two came into the room, that you must have another transfusion of blood, and that both you and he were exhausted. Now I know well that you medical men speak in camera, and that a man must not expect to know what they consult about in private. But this is no common matter, and, whatever it is, I have done my part. Is not that so?"
He wants to know what is wrong with Lucy, though his own hopes of marrying her are in the past. He has already given help, so he feels he has a right to be told.

She told me that, if she might, she would come presently to my study, as she had much to say. So here I am finishing my entry in my phonograph diary whilst I await her. As yet I have not had the chance of looking at the papers which Van Helsing left with me, though they lie open before me. I must get her interested in something, so that I may have an opportunity of reading them. She does not know how precious time is, or what a task we have in hand. I must be careful not to frighten her. Here she is!

What is the narrator planning in this diary entry?
He is waiting for a visitor to come to his study. He wants to read the papers that Van Helsing left, so he plans to get her interested in something else. He must be careful not to frighten her.

What did the group decide to do that night?

After a general discussion it was determined that for to-night nothing be definitely settled; that we should all sleep on the facts, and try to think out the proper conclusions. To-morrow, at breakfast, we are to meet again, and, after making our conclusions known to one another, we shall decide on some definite cause of action.
They decided to settle nothing yet and to sleep on the facts. Tomorrow at breakfast they will share their conclusions and then choose a definite plan.

And now we are all scattered; and for many a long day loneliness will sit over our roofs with brooding wings. Lucy lies in the tomb of her kin, a lordly death-house in a lonely churchyard, away from teeming London; where the air is fresh, and the sun rises over Hampstead Hill, and where wild flowers grow of their own accord.

How does the writer describe the place where Lucy rests?
She lies in the tomb of her family, a grand death-house in a lonely churchyard far from busy London. The air is fresh, the sun rises over Hampstead Hill, and wild flowers grow there.

Who attended the funeral, and how did Mina and Jonathan feel?

The service was very simple and very solemn. There were only ourselves and the servants there, one or two old friends of his from Exeter, his London agent, and a gentleman representing Sir John Paxton, the President of the Incorporated Law Society. Jonathan and I stood hand in hand, and we felt that our best and dearest friend was gone from us....

Only a few: themselves, the servants, some old friends from Exeter, a London agent and a representative of the law society. Mina and Jonathan stood hand in hand, feeling they had lost their best friend.

As we came home we could arrive at no definite conclusion. We were all convinced that the box was on its way, by water, to somewhere; but where that might be we would have to discover. With heavy hearts we came home to the hotel to Mina.

What had the group worked out by the end of the day?
They agreed the box was on its way somewhere by water, but they did not know where. They went back to the hotel and to Mina with heavy hearts.

What do the wounds on the children have in common, and what do the police do?

There is, however, possibly a serious side to the question, for some of the children, indeed all who have been missed at night, have been slightly torn or wounded in the throat. The wounds seem such as might be made by a rat or a small dog, and although of not much importance individually, would tend to show that whatever animal inflicts them has a system or method of its own. The police of the division have been instructed to keep a sharp look-out for straying children, especially when very young, in and around Hampstead Heath, and for any stray dog which may be about.

Every child missed at night has a small tear in the throat, like a bite from a rat or small dog, which suggests a method. The police are told to watch for straying children and stray dogs near Hampstead Heath.

"Meanwhile Kunti seeing that her sons were late in returning from their eleemosynary round, was filled with anxiety. She began to think of various evils having overtaken her sons. At one time she thought that the sons of Dhritarashtra having recognised her sons had slain them. Next she feared that some cruel and strong Rakshasas endued with powers of deception had slain them. And she asked herself, 'Could the illustrious Vyasa himself (who had directed my sons to come to Panchala) have been guided by perverse intelligence?' Thus reflected Pritha in consequence of her affection for her offspring. Then in the stillness of the late afternoon, Jishnu, accompanied by a body of Brahmanas, entered the abode of the potter, like the cloud-covered sun appearing on a cloudy day.'"

Why is Kunti anxious in this passage?
Her sons are late from begging, so she imagines terrible things: that Dhritarashtra's sons had found and killed them, or that Rakshasas had. Then Arjuna arrives with the Brahmanas.

What does Vidura ask the Rishi to do?

Vaisampayana said, "Then Vidura began to think of that Rishi of rigid vows. And knowing that he was thought of, the Rishi, O Bharata, showed himself there. Vidura then received him with the rites prescribed by ordinance. And when, having rested a while, the Rishi was seated at his ease, Vidura addressed him, saying, 'O illustrious one, there is a doubt in Dhritarashtra's mind which is incapable of being explained away by me. It behooveth thee, therefore, to expound it, so that listening to thy discourse, this chief of men may tide over all this sorrows, and to that gain and loss, what is agreeable and what disagreeable, decrepitude and death, fright and jealously, hunger and thirst, pride and prosperity, dislike, sleep, lust and wrath, and decrease and increase may all be borne by him!'"
He asks the Rishi to clear up a doubt in Dhritarashtra's mind that Vidura cannot explain. He hopes the king, by listening, will be able to bear sorrow, loss, old age and death.

"Arjuna said, 'Sikhandin, O Krishna, will certainly be the cause of Bhishma's death, for Bhishma, as soon as he beholds the prince of the Panchalas, abstains from striking. Therefore, keeping Sikhandin before him and at our head, we will, by that means, overthrow the son of Ganga. Even this is what I think. I will hold in check other great bowmen with my shafts. As regards Sikhandin, he will fight with Bhishma alone, that foremost of all warriors. I have heard from that chief of the Kurus that he would not strike Sikhandin, for having been born before as a woman he subsequently became a male person.'"

Why does Arjuna want Sikhandin placed in front of Bhishma?
Arjuna says Bhishma will not strike him, because Sikhandin was born a woman before becoming a man. So Sikhandin can face Bhishma while Arjuna holds back the other great bowmen.

What does Arjuna tell Uttara to do on the way back?

Vaisampayana continued, "When all the Kauravas utterly routed and vanquished, set out in a dejected mood for Hastinapura, Falguna, on his way back, addressed Uttara, saying, 'O prince, O hero of mighty arms, seeing the kine escorted in advance of us by the cowherds, we shall enter Virata's metropolis in the afternoon, having tended the steeds with drink and a bath. Let the cowherds, despatched by thee, speedily repair to the city with the good news and proclaim thy victory.'"
He tells him to send the cowherds ahead to the city with the good news of the victory. The two will follow in the afternoon, after the horses have had a drink and a bath.

Vaisampayana continued, "Then Virata's son began to describe the prowess of Arjuna, saying, 'Even this one is he that slew the foe, like unto a lion devastating a flock of deer. Even he ranged through crowds of hostile cars, slaying their best of car-warriors. By him was slain a huge, infuriate elephant by means of a single arrow. Pierced by him, that huge beast having its flanks adorned with an armour of gold, fell down piercing the earth with his tusks. By him have the kine been recovered and the Kauravas vanquished in battle. My ears have been deafened by the blare of his conch. It was by this hero of fierce deeds that Bhishma and Drona, along with Duryodhana, were vanquished. That achievement is his and not mine.'"

Whom does Uttara give credit for the victory?
He gives it to Arjuna, not himself. He lists how this hero killed an elephant with one arrow, recovered the cows and defeated Bhishma, Drona and Duryodhana, and says the achievement is not his.

What does Dhritarashtra believe about destiny and effort?

Dhritarashtra said, "Tell me, O Sanjaya, how that great bowman Drona and the Panchala prince of Prishata's race encounter each other in battle, each striving his best. I regard destiny to be superior, O Sanjaya, to exertion, when Santanu's son Bhishma (even) could not escape Pandu's son in battle. Indeed, Bhishma, when enraged in battle could destroy all mobile and immobile creatures, why, O Sanjaya, could he not then by his prowess, escape the son of Pandu in battle?"
He thinks destiny is stronger than effort. As proof, he asks how Bhishma, who could destroy all creatures when angry, could not escape the son of Pandu in battle.

Saurabh, okay, you caught me. Yes, I got selected for the national science olympiad. The letter came during Diwali, right when everyone was at our house. Mummy wanted to announce it at dinner and I begged her not to. When my friends asked on the group chat, I wrote, "Lol, fluke, the paper was easy." It wasn't easy. I worked on it for months. But I've seen what happens. When Rohit got into that music school, people started calling him "Mr Big Shot" and stopped inviting him. I don't want that. So I joke about it. But honestly, it feels bad, making my own work sound like nothing. I'm, like, proud and scared at the same time. I, Manoj, am the olympiad guy. And I'm hiding it.

Why does Manoj joke about his olympiad selection?
He has seen friends teased and left out after succeeding, like Rohit. So he calls it a fluke to avoid that, though he knows he worked for months and feels both proud and scared.

What does Lalremsiami realise about her worries over her skin?

Dear Jeevan, You asked why I didn't want to come to the Christmas youth fellowship. Honestly, it's my skin. This month it's been really bad, and I'm sure every person in church stares at it. When the choir leader looked at me during practice, I thought, she thinks I'm disgusting. When two boys whispered, I knew it was about me. Then yesterday my friend said, "You're so quiet lately, is something wrong?" Nobody had even mentioned my face. I think the only one saying mean things about my skin is me. It's strange how loud my own voice sounds when it pretends to be everyone else's. Maybe I'll come on Sunday. Lalremsiami
She sees that no one has mentioned her skin, and that the unkind voice is her own, imagining what others think. That is why she thinks she might come on Sunday.

Siddharth, you want money for each book you read? Let me tell you what happened to your Pradeep dadu. When I was nine, I loved books so much that my mother had to pull them out of my hands at dinner. Then my uncle, meaning well, said he'd give me four annas for every book I finished. Oh, I was rich within a month! But I stopped choosing the thick adventure books with maps. I chose the thinnest ones in the school cupboard, the ones for small children. I finished them on the bus. I couldn't tell you a single story from them. One day I realised I hadn't opened my favourite pirate book in weeks. I asked my uncle to stop the annas. It took me a whole summer to love reading again.

What went wrong when the uncle paid him for each book?
He began choosing the thinnest children's books to earn money faster and remembered nothing from them. He stopped enjoying his favourite pirate book, and it took a summer to love reading again.

What advice does Zeenat Aunty give about learning to draw?

Chetan beta, you want to draw like me? Then hear how your Zeenat Aunty started, back when she was nine and owned one pencil. My friend Shabnam and I got drawing books in the same week. Shabnam made a grand plan: two hours every evening, a new portrait each day. I looked at my evenings, full of homework and fetching water, and I thought, two hours will break by Wednesday. So I said ten minutes, right after the evening prayer, every single day. Shabnam's plan lasted three evenings. Mine lasted, well, look at these hands. Some days ten minutes was only one leaf. But a leaf every day for a year makes a whole tree, beta.
Make a small plan you can keep. She drew for ten minutes every day, while her friend's two-hour plan lasted three evenings. Small daily steps add up, like a leaf each day making a tree.

In the clinic waiting room, Rajni pulled her hand out of her mother's. "I can sit alone." When the nurse called her name, she marched in first, chin up. The injection pricked; her eyes filled, but she pressed her lips together and stared at the chart of animals on the wall. Damini reached out to hug her. Rajni twisted away and climbed down from the bed herself. Only in the auto home, when she thought no one was looking, did a tear slide down, and she rubbed it off quickly.

What does Rajni's behaviour show about how she feels?
She wants to look brave and independent, so she walks in first, refuses a hug and climbs down alone. But she cries quietly in the auto and wipes the tear away when she thinks no one is looking.

Why did Vaibhav wait before speaking to Madhav?

Mentor's note, new-joiner programme, Friday. Vaibhav has been keen to meet people on other teams. This morning he wanted to ask Madhav from finance about the budget tool. I saw him walk toward Madhav's desk, then stop. Madhav had his earphones in, was typing fast, and had two coffee cups beside him, clearly racing a deadline. Vaibhav turned back and sat down. At lunch, Madhav was sitting alone, earphones off, stretching. Vaibhav went over. "Hi, I'm Vaibhav, new in operations. Do you have five minutes sometime about the budget tool?" Madhav smiled. "Sit, I've got ten now. This morning was madness." They talked for twenty minutes. Afterwards I mentioned to Vaibhav that waiting was a good call. He said he didn't want to be the person who interrupts.
Madhav was wearing earphones and typing fast near a deadline, so Vaibhav did not want to interrupt. At lunch he asked politely for five minutes, and Madhav gave him ten.

Parul's journalism tutorial was stuck on a short piece about a canteen price rise. The tutor, Harish, asked each student to underline facts in blue and opinions in red. Parul found "The price rose from twenty to twenty-five rupees" in blue, and "students are outraged" in red, since no one had been quoted. She raised her hand. "Who was asked? How many?" The writer, a classmate, admitted he'd asked two friends. Parul felt her worry about being blunt fade when Harish nodded and said that was the exact question. The writer went red but agreed to add a proper count and a line from the canteen manager.

What question does Parul ask about the canteen article, and why does it matter?
She asks who was asked and how many. The claim that students are outraged has no quotes, so it is only opinion. The writer had asked just two friends, so the piece needs a proper count.

Why did Trisha think Ayesha was ignoring her?

I sit near the pantry at the design studio, so I see everyone come in. On Monday Ayesha walked in late, phone at her ear, arms full of fabric samples. Across the room Trisha looked up from her screen. Ayesha couldn't wave or call out, so she lifted both eyebrows quickly, a little flash with half a smile, and kept walking to the meeting room. Trisha didn't notice; she had already looked back down. I only caught it because I was pouring tea. At lunch Ayesha stopped by Trisha's desk. "Hey, sorry, I did say hi this morning. Sort of. With my eyebrows." Trisha laughed. "Honestly? I thought you were ignoring me." I can't say what either of them was feeling, but they ate together after that, and Ayesha said a proper good morning on Tuesday.
Ayesha could only raise her eyebrows with half a smile because her hands and phone were busy, and Trisha had already looked down and missed it. They cleared it up at lunch.

At the community centre reception, Sangeeta had been telling Ritu about her grandson's school play for a long stretch, from the costume to the missing prop to the teacher's speech. Ritu nodded, glancing at the clock over the door and at the chairs still stacked for the afternoon class. At the next pause Ritu said, "So the prop turned up in the end and he got the biggest clap. That's lovely, thank you for telling me. I have to set out the chairs for the afternoon class now. Will you tell me the rest at chai tomorrow?" "Oh, I do go on," said Sangeeta, laughing. "Not at all. I want to hear it," said Ritu.

How does Ritu end the long story politely?
She sums up what Sangeeta told her, thanks her and explains she must set out chairs. Then she invites her to tell the rest at chai tomorrow, so Sangeeta feels welcome.

How does Parveen cope when she misses a week of work?

Dear Ujjwal, You asked how the book is going. Here's the honest version. Big aim: finish my Urdu picture book about the kite-seller and send it to three publishers by December. Monthly: March, the story. April and May, twelve sketches. June, final text. And so on. Weekly: two sketches and one page of text, every Sunday morning with chai. Every Sunday night I look back at the week. Not to scold myself. Just: what got done, what didn't, what changes. Two weeks ago Ammi was unwell and I did nothing at all. Old me would have given up. Instead I wrote 'Missed. Fine. Move April's sketches into May.' And carried on. I'm on sketch nine now. It might be a month late. It's still going to happen. Come and meet the kite-seller when you visit. Parveen
She writes "Missed. Fine." and moves the April sketches to May, then carries on. She looks back every Sunday without scolding herself, so the plan bends instead of breaking.

"Raghav, stay back a minute?" Jeevan, the geography teacher, said as the others ran out. Raghav froze by the door. "Did I do something?" "No. I read your answer on why the river changes course. Two pages. Nobody else thought about the farmers." Raghav looked at his shoes. "I knew it in class. The words just get stuck when everyone turns round." "That's all right. You haven't raised your hand once this term, and I'd started to wonder if geography bored you." "It's my favourite." "Then here's a deal. Every Friday, write me one question or idea on a slip. I'll read the good ones out, without your name if you like." "With my name," Raghav said quietly. "Maybe."

What does Jeevan notice about Raghav, and what does he offer?
He noticed Raghav's thoughtful answer about the farmers and that he never raises his hand. He offers a Friday slip for a question or idea, which he will read out with or without a name.

What does Kwame learn about Wei?

The group project for Urban Planning met every Tuesday at nine in the Manchester university library, and every Tuesday Wei was late or yawning. By week four Kwame had had enough. "He's just lazy," he told the other two. "He does the bare minimum and sleeps through meetings." He started writing Wei's sections himself. Then one Friday at six in the morning, Kwame went to the big supermarket near the station for milk. At the loading bay, in a grey uniform, stacking crates onto a trolley, was Wei. He looked exhausted. He saw Kwame and gave a small, awkward wave. "Night shift," Wei said. "Five nights a week. My rent." Kwame stood holding his milk and thought of every Tuesday he had called him lazy.
Wei works five night shifts a week at a supermarket to pay his rent, so he is tired on Tuesdays. Kwame had called him lazy and now thinks about every time he judged him wrongly.

When the first monsoon rain hit their village near Bhopal, Rehana, twenty months, was on the verandah. Sumit, the neighbour's boy, ran out into it, stamping. Rehana stared, then held her hand out past the roof. Cold drops. She shrieked and pulled it back, then stuck it out again, laughing. Her Ammi carried her to the edge of a puddle. Rehana stamped once, twice, and splashed Sumit. They both collapsed into giggles.

How does Rehana react to her first monsoon rain?
She stares, holds her hand out into the rain, shrieks at the cold drops and pulls it back, then does it again, laughing. Later she stamps in a puddle and splashes Sumit, and they giggle.

How does Santosh help his grandfather with the repeated question?

Santosh, nine, watched Dada take a long time to cross the living room of their Lucknow flat, leaning on his stick. Then Dada asked, "Who won the match?" He had asked that ten minutes ago. Santosh went to the kitchen. "Papa, is Dada very sick?" he whispered. Deepak dried his hands. "Dada's body is old now, beta. His legs are weaker and sometimes he forgets things. It's not his fault. He's still our Dada." "Is he scared?" "Sometimes, I think. That's why we're gentle." Santosh went back and sat on the floor by Dada's chair. "Dada, shall I read you the cricket page?" Dada smiled and patted his head. Santosh read slowly, and when Dada asked about the match again, he just read the score once more.
He asks his father why Dada forgets, learns that it is because of age and not his fault, then reads him the cricket page. When Dada asks again, he patiently reads the score once more.
